meaning: Someone doesn't say it, but their attitude or actions make it obvious, as if they were saying “...”.
connection: Quoted phrase + とばかりに／と言わんばかりに (の)

senses.label: As if to say
senses.meaning: What comes before is what the other person seems to want to say. Used to describe someone's look or behavior. Vivid; mostly in narration and writing.
senses.connection: Quoted phrase (command, exclamation, 「今だ」, etc.) + とばかりに + action; common set phrases: 「待ってましたとばかりに」, 「ここぞとばかりに」
examples: He opened the door as if to say, “Go home already.”
As if to say “Now's our chance!”, the players all charged forward at once.
As if they'd been waiting for this moment, the kids pounced on the snacks.

senses.label: All but saying it
senses.meaning: 「と言わんばかり」 is stronger: “they didn't say it, but they practically did.” Use 「の」 before a noun.
senses.connection: Quoted phrase + と言わんばかりに + verb／と言わんばかりの + noun (顔, 態度, 目つき, etc.)
examples: The clerk's attitude practically said, “Hurry up and leave.”
She glared at me as if to say it was all my fault.

notes: Use it only to describe a third person's look or behavior, never the speaker's own: ✕「私はもう帰れとばかりにドアを開けた」. To state your own intention, say it directly: ○「早く帰ってほしくて、ドアを開けた」.

「〜とばかり思っていた」 means “I had been thinking all along that...” and is a different pattern. Mixing them up changes the meaning completely: 「彼は独身だとばかり思っていた」 is “I always assumed he was single,” not “he seemed to be saying he was single.”
「言わん」 is a fixed archaic form and cannot be modernized: ✕「言うばかりに」「言わないばかりに」 → ○「言わんばかりに」. Before a noun, use 「の」: ○「言わんばかりの顔」.

「〜と言わんばかりの態度／顔」 is mostly used to criticize someone's impatience, contempt, or arrogance. Saying 「早く帰れと言わんばかりですね」 to someone's face accuses them of a bad attitude, which is very rude toward a superior or a customer.

daily.title: The family cat
daily.description: Telling the family what the cat is doing when its owner comes home.
daily.example: The cat keeps meowing as if to say, “Feed me.”

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: Novels often use this to describe a character's manner.
daily.example: The man stood up as if to say the conversation was over.

daily.title: Complaining to a friend
daily.description: Telling a friend about a clerk's cold attitude.
daily.example: That shop started cleaning up as if to say, “We're closed.”

work.title: News report
work.description: A sports report describing a turning point in a game.
work.example: When the opponent made a mistake, the team seized the moment and went on the attack.

work.title: The mood in a meeting
work.description: Coworkers privately discussing the boss's attitude in a meeting.
work.example: The department head closed the documents with a look that said, “No objections allowed.”

etymology: 「と」 marks a quote, and 「ばかり」 means “to the extent of, almost.” The 「ん」 in 「言わんばかり」 is a sound change of the classical auxiliary 「む」 (conjecture). Literally: “to the point of almost saying it.”

similar.title: 〜んばかりに／〜んばかりの
similar.explanation: Same origin: both contain 「ばかり」 (degree) and the archaic 「ん」. 「〜んばかりに」 attaches to the stem of the verb's ない-form and means “almost doing something” (「泣かんばかりに頼む」); 「〜とばかりに」 follows an unspoken line (「帰れとばかりに」). 「と言わんばかり」 is simply 「言う」 plus 「んばかり」.

similar.title: 〜かのようだ
similar.explanation: Close in meaning (“as if...”). 「〜かのように」 is a general comparison that can follow many kinds of situations (「何もなかったかのように」); 「〜とばかりに」 is specifically for “reading” an unspoken line in someone's attitude or actions, so a quoted phrase comes before it.

formation: It has three parts: 「と」, which marks quoted content; 「ばかり」, meaning “to the extent of, almost”; and 「に」, which turns the whole into an adverb modifying the action that follows. What comes before 「と」 is a “line of dialogue,” but 「ばかり」 only says “to that degree,” so nobody has actually said it. The whole means “the look or action is so clear that it is as if the person were saying that line.” 「と言わんばかり」 inserts 「言わ」 (the 未然形 of 「言う」) + 「ん」 (the archaic conjecture auxiliary 「む」), literally “on the verge of saying ‘...’,” which is more direct and stronger than 「とばかり」. Because the line is something an onlooker “reads” from another person's behavior, it is used only for other people. Use 「に」 to modify a verb and 「の」 to modify a noun (顔, 態度).

meaning: Doing something without really meaning to; after a question word, it means you can't tell who, where, or when.
connection: Verb dictionary form + ともなく (ともなしに)／question word (+ particle) + ともなく

senses.label: Absent-mindedly
senses.meaning: Doing something casually, without a clear purpose. The same verb is often repeated before and after. Common with 「見る・聞く・言う・考える・待つ」.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + ともなく／ともなしに + same verb (「見るともなく見る」, 「聞くともなしに聞く」)
examples: I was idly watching TV when a song I remembered fondly came on.
I couldn't help overhearing the conversation at the next table.
I was gazing out the window at nothing in particular.

senses.label: From nowhere / no one knows who
senses.meaning: After a question word, it means you can't pin down who, where from, or when. Mostly set phrases.
senses.connection: どこから／誰から／いつから／どこへ + ともなく
examples: A nice smell drifted in from somewhere.
Applause broke out, though no one knew who started it.
He left for who knows where.

notes: It means “without really intending to,” so it cannot be combined with words that imply deliberate or careful action such as 「わざわざ」「一生懸命」「じっくり」: ✕「じっくり見るともなく見た」.

The same verb is normally repeated before and after, and it is mostly limited to perception and thought verbs like 「見る・聞く・言う・考える・待つ」. It sounds unnatural with ordinary actions like 「食べる」「書く」; to say “did it casually,” use 「なんとなく」.
With a question word it is not a negation: 「誰からともなく拍手が起こった」 means “applause started, though no one could say who began it,” not “nobody clapped.” 「どこへともなく去った」 means “went off to who knows where.”
Do not confuse it with the similar-looking 「〜とも」 (“even if”): 「何があろうとも」 means “no matter what happens” and has nothing to do with doing something unintentionally.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: A novel describing a character lost in thought.
daily.example: She was listening absently to the sound of the rain.

daily.title: Explaining what you overheard
daily.description: Telling a friend you weren't eavesdropping on purpose.
daily.example: I was half listening on the train, and they turned out to be talking about someone I know.

daily.title: An evening street
daily.description: Describing the mood in a diary or essay.
daily.example: The smell of dinner drifted over from somewhere.

work.title: Newspaper column
work.description: Essays and columns often use this literary expression.
work.example: In the hall, a moment of silence began without anyone in particular starting it.

work.title: News report
work.description: Describing something that happened naturally in a crowd.
work.example: People gathered in the square from all directions.

etymology: Made of the quoting particle 「と」, the particle 「も」, and 「なく」 (from 「ない」). Literally “not even to the point of saying ‘I'll do it’”, which came to mean “unintentionally, absently”.

similar.title: 〜ままに(as one pleases)
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both can describe doing something casually, without a clear purpose. 「気の向くままに歩く」 stresses following one's mood and letting things take their course; 「歩くともなく歩く」 stresses that you are barely aware of doing the action at all. 「ままに」 can follow 「noun + の」, while 「ともなく」 repeats the same verb before and after.

similar.title: 〜のやら・〜ものやら・〜ことやら
similar.explanation: Close in meaning to 「question word + ともなく」: both carry the sense of “can't say for sure...”. 「何を考えているのやら」 comes at the end of a sentence and expresses the speaker's bewilderment or sigh about something unclear; 「どこからともなく」 modifies the action that follows and merely describes, objectively, that the source is unknown, with no sigh.

formation: It is built from the quotative 「と」 + the particle 「も」 + 「なく」, the 連用形 of 「ない」. 「AするともなくAする」 literally means “doing A without it even amounting to ‘I'm going to do A’”: 「と」 brings out the intention to do it as content, and 「も…なく」 negates it. The action remains but the intention is removed, giving “doing it unintentionally, absent-mindedly.” Since what is negated is the intention, not the action, the same verb is usually repeated. With a question word (「どこからともなく」), what 「と」 brings out and negates is the answer to “from where,” i.e. “you can't say from where,” so it expresses an unknown source or target. 「ともなしに」 just swaps 「なく」 for the archaic 「なし」; the structure is the same, but it is more literary.

meaning: Once someone or something reaches a higher status, age, period, or level, a matching situation naturally follows.
connection: Noun／verb dictionary form + ともなると／ともなれば

senses.label: At that level
senses.meaning: The first part is an age, position, time of year, etc. It means “at this level, things are different.” The second part is a judgment like “naturally ...”.
senses.connection: Noun (大学生・社長・十二月・プロ, etc.) + ともなると／ともなれば
examples: Once you're a university student, you have to make your own decisions.
When you're the company president, you probably can't relax even on days off.
When December comes, the whole town is full of Christmas.

senses.label: When it actually comes to doing it
senses.meaning: After a verb, it means “when it actually comes to doing this.” It stresses how big a deal it is and how things change. Often used with 「いざ」.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + ともなると／ともなれば (often 「いざ〜ともなると」)
examples: When it actually comes to buying a house, you have no choice but to be careful.
If you're going to live abroad on your own, there's a mountain of things to prepare.

notes: The first clause must be a status, period, or matter that the speaker regards as “high-level” or “weighty.” For an ordinary condition, use 「〜となると」: ✕「雨ともなると、試合は中止だ」 → ○「雨となると、試合は中止だ」.

It differs from 「〜ともあろう」 by one word but means something different: 「社長ともなると忙しい」 is an objective judgment (“once you're a company president, naturally you're busy”); 「社長ともあろう人が嘘をつくなんて」 is a rebuke (“how could someone who is a company president lie”). Using the wrong one turns a neutral statement into criticism.

The second clause is a judgment or conjecture that “once things reach this stage, this is naturally how it is,” and it does not take the speaker's commands or requests: ✕「大学生ともなると、自分で考えなさい」 → ○「大学生ともなれば、自分で考えるべきだ」.

daily.title: Kids growing up
daily.description: Parents chatting about how their kids change as they grow.
daily.example: Once they're in junior high, they don't talk to their parents much, do they?

daily.title: Talking about the season
daily.description: Chatting with a friend about the year-end rush.
daily.example: At the end of the year, every shop is crowded.

daily.title: Planning a wedding
daily.description: Friends discussing wedding preparations.
daily.example: When you actually get married, there's so much to decide. It's exhausting.

work.title: Management duties
work.description: A senior colleague explaining a manager's responsibilities to someone just promoted.
work.example: Once you're in management, guiding your staff becomes an important part of the job.

work.title: News commentary
work.description: Commenting on the scale of a major event.
work.example: For something like the Olympics, the economic effect reaches several trillion yen.

etymology: Made of the quoting particle 「と」, the emphatic 「も」, and the conditional forms of 「なる」 (「と」, 「ば」). Here 「も」 adds emphasis: “it has actually reached this level.”

similar.title: 〜となると・〜となれば・〜となったら
similar.explanation: Same origin, just without the emphatic particle 「も」. 「〜となると」 is more neutral and can follow ordinary situations (「雨となると中止だ」); 「〜ともなると」 uses 「も」 to stress that the first clause is of a high, extraordinary level (「社長ともなると」).

similar.title: 〜ともあろう
similar.explanation: Same origin: it is also built from 「と＋も」 and also follows a status or position. 「〜ともあろう＋人」 means “someone as prominent as ... and yet...” and carries surprise or censure; 「〜ともなると」 just explains what naturally happens once that stage is reached, with no criticism.

formation: It is built from the quotative 「と」 + the emphatic particle 「も」 + the conditional forms 「なると／なれば」 of the verb 「なる」 (“to become”). 「Aとなると」 already means “once it becomes A (in that situation).” Inserting 「も」 works like “even, as far as” in English, stressing “to the point of being as high as A,” so the first clause is naturally understood as a high, out-of-the-ordinary stage. Since 「なる」 expresses a change of state, the whole carries the nuance “as you reach this stage, things change accordingly,” and the second clause is usually a judgment such as “naturally ...”. 「なれば」 is slightly more hypothetical than 「なると」.

meaning: Even if something doesn't reach a high level, it should at least reach a somewhat lower one.
connection: Verb nai-form + までも (nouns／na-adjectives: 「〜でないまでも／〜とは言わないまでも」)

senses.label: At least
senses.meaning: The first part is the higher standard; the second is the minimum you'll settle for. The second part usually expresses a wish, duty, or intention. Often paired with 「せめて」, 「少なくとも」, or 「〜ぐらいは」.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form + までも + 〜てほしい／〜べきだ／〜たい
examples: I won't say every day, but I'd like you to call at least once a week.
Even if we can't win the championship, I want to make the top eight.
Even if it isn't perfect, you should do a certain amount of preparation.

senses.label: Not quite ..., but still
senses.meaning: The second part is an evaluation or a fact: “it can't quite be called ..., but it's still pretty ...”. Often 「〜とは言えないまでも」.
senses.connection: 〜とは言えないまでも／〜ほどではないまでも + evaluation
examples: He may not be a professional, but his cooking is pretty impressive.
It wasn't a huge success, but the event turned out reasonably well.

notes: The first clause must be a higher level than the second; reversed, it makes no sense: ✕「ベスト8に入れないまでも、優勝したい」 → ○「優勝できないまでも、ベスト8には入りたい」.

It differs from 「〜までもない」 only in word order, but the meaning is completely different: 「説明しないまでも」 is “even if you don't explain in detail, at least...”; 「説明するまでもない」 is “there's no need to explain.” The former takes the ない-form, the latter the dictionary form.

It carries a “stepping down, lowering the demand” nuance. Saying 「毎日とは言わないまでも、週に一度は報告してください」 to a superior or a client sounds like a complaint that they aren't doing enough; for a formal request, say 「週に一度ご報告いただけますと助かります」.

daily.title: Asking family for something
daily.description: A mother asking her child who lives alone to keep in touch.
daily.example: I won't say every day, but get in touch once in a while.

daily.title: Praising a friend's baking
daily.description: Complimenting a cake a friend made.
daily.example: It's not quite bakery level, but it's really good!

daily.title: Setting a goal
daily.description: A student talking about exam goals.
daily.example: Even if I can't get a perfect score, I want at least 80.

work.title: Project review
work.description: Reporting project results to a manager.
work.example: While we cannot say we have reached our target, we have achieved a certain level of results.

work.title: Setting a minimum
work.description: Stating a minimum requirement for the team in a meeting.
work.example: Even if we don't do a full review, we need to check where the problems are.

etymology: Made of the negative 「ない」 plus the particles 「まで」 (extent) and 「も」. Literally “even if it doesn't go as far as ...”, which came to mean “at the very least ...”.

similar.title: 〜にしても
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both can express “even if..., (at least)...”. 「優勝できないにしても、ベスト8には入りたい」 is also possible, but 「にしても」 is just an ordinary concession; 「ないまでも」 explicitly treats the first clause as a high standard out of reach, and the second as the minimum one falls back on.

similar.title: 〜くらい・〜ぐらい(minimum, belittling)
similar.explanation: Close in meaning and often used together. 「〜ぐらい（は）」 directly names “at least this much” as the minimum (「電話ぐらいしてほしい」); 「〜ないまでも」 first raises a high standard that is not met, then introduces the minimum: 「毎日とは言わないまでも、電話ぐらいしてほしい」.

similar.title: 〜までもない・〜までもなく
similar.explanation: Same origin: also built from 「まで＋も」, yet the meaning is entirely different. 「〜までもない」 follows the dictionary form of a verb and means “there is no need to...” (「言うまでもない」); 「〜ないまでも」 follows the ない-form and means “even if it doesn't reach..., at least...”.

formation: It is built from the negative auxiliary 「ない」 + the particle 「まで」 (limit) + the concessive 「も」. 「Aないまで」 means “not reaching the point of A,” and adding 「も」 makes it “even if it doesn't reach the point of A,” as though the high standard A is conceded first. The speaker steps back, so the second clause naturally lands on a lower standard, which is why it often pairs with 「せめて」「少なくとも」「ぐらいは」. Precisely because it steps down from A, the second item must be lower in degree than the first. 「とは言わないまでも」 concedes the act of calling it A: “I won't say it's A, but at least...”.

meaning: A double negative meaning “it's not that I won't/can't ...”: possible under certain conditions, with a hedging tone.
connection: Verb nai-form + ものでもない／でもない

senses.label: Not out of the question
senses.meaning: Depending on conditions, it could happen. The tone is reluctant and avoids a clear promise. Often with 「条件次第では」 or 「〜なら」.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form + ものでもない (often 「〜なら／〜次第では〜ないものでもない」)
examples: Depending on the terms, I might be willing to take it on.
If we hurry, it's not impossible to make it in time.
If you're going to push it that far, I suppose I could help.

senses.label: Sort of / somewhat
senses.meaning: Often with verbs of feeling or understanding: “to some small degree.” A soft way to avoid stating something outright.
senses.connection: Nai-form of わかる・思う・感じる・気がする, etc. + でもない
examples: I can kind of understand how he feels.
Now that you mention it, I do sort of feel that way.
I do think it's a bit expensive, but oh well.

notes: This is a double negative meaning “grudging yes,” so using it to agree to someone's request sounds reluctant and condescending. Answering a superior or client with 「引き受けないものでもありません」 is rude; say 「お引き受けいたします」 or 「条件によってはお引き受けできます」.
Do not read it as a negation: 「手伝わないものでもない」 means “I might help,” not “I won't help”; 「行かないでもない」 means “it's not that I won't go.”
Do not confuse it with the partial negation 「〜わけではない」: 「嫌いなわけではない」 means “it's not that I dislike it,” while 「わからないでもない」 means “it's not that I don't understand (I understand somewhat).”
To say “I kind of feel...,” use 「〜ないでもない」: ○「気持ちはわからないでもない」. 「わからないものでもない」 sounds stiff; 「〜ないものでもない」 is mostly used for the possibility that you yourself would do something under certain conditions.

daily.title: A friend asks a favor
daily.description: A friend keeps begging, and you reluctantly give in.
daily.example: If you're begging that much, I guess I could lend it to you.

daily.title: Understanding someone
daily.description: Listening to a friend explain why they want to quit their job.
daily.example: I can sort of understand why you'd want to quit.

daily.title: Thinking about buying
daily.description: Wondering in a shop whether to buy something.
daily.example: At this price, I might buy it.

work.title: Business negotiation
work.description: Keeping options open about the other side's terms.
work.example: If you could extend the delivery date, we would not be unwilling to accept.

work.title: Assessing feasibility
work.description: Discussing whether a plan is possible in a meeting.
work.example: If we add more staff, finishing within the year isn't impossible.

etymology: Made of the negative 「ない」, the formal noun 「もの」, and 「でもない」: “it isn't the kind of thing I won't do.” Two negatives combine into a hedged positive.

similar.title: 〜なくもない／〜なくはない
similar.explanation: Almost the same meaning: “it's not that...not.” 「〜なくもない」 is the most colloquial and can also follow adjectives; 「〜ないものでもない」 is the most literary and stiff, mostly about the possibility that you yourself would do something under certain conditions.

similar.title: 〜ないことはない
similar.explanation: Close in meaning. 「〜ないことはない」 is more colloquial and slightly more affirmative, and can express objective possibility (「急げば間に合わないことはない」); 「〜ないものでもない」 is more literary and more grudging and reserved.

similar.title: 〜ないとも限らない
similar.explanation: Also a double negative and often compared, but it goes the other way: 「〜ないとも限らない」 means “it can't be guaranteed that it won't...”, mostly for worrying that something bad may happen and urging caution; 「〜ないものでもない」 mostly means that you yourself might do something under certain conditions.

formation: It is a two-layer negation: 「ない」 + the formal noun 「もの」 + 「でもない」. 「Aないもの」 means “the kind of thing where one doesn't do A,” and 「でもない」 denies that again: “it isn't a case of not doing A either.” It takes two detours to come back to the affirmative. Because it never directly says “do it” and only rules out “not doing it,” it expresses a conditional, grudging affirmation that leaves room for reservation. 「〜ないでもない」, with 「もの」 dropped, has the same structure but is more colloquial and mostly follows verbs of feeling or recognition, meaning “somewhat...”.

meaning: Keeping a certain state unchanged: “with ...”, “by birth”, or “just as it has always been”.
connection: Noun／verb masu-stem + ながらに (ながらの + noun)

senses.label: By birth
senses.meaning: 「生まれながらに」 means “from birth, innately.” Formal; often used for talents or rights.
senses.connection: 生まれながらに (して)／生まれながらの + noun
examples: He was born with an outstanding talent for music.
All people are born equal.

senses.label: In tears
senses.meaning: 「涙ながらに」 means doing something while crying. Often with 「語る・訴える・謝る」.
senses.connection: 涙ながらに + verb of speaking
examples: She told us about the incident in tears.
The victim's mother made a tearful appeal.

senses.label: As in the old days
senses.meaning: 「昔ながらの」 means something has stayed the same as in the past, usually with nostalgia or praise. 「いつもながらの」 means “as always”.
senses.connection: 昔ながらの／いつもながらの + noun
examples: This town still has its old-fashioned streets.
This is miso made by traditional methods.
It was a brilliant performance, as always.

senses.label: Without leaving home
senses.meaning: 「いながらにして」 means you can do something without moving from where you are. Common when talking about modern technology.
senses.connection: (家に) いながらにして + something possible
examples: Thanks to the internet, you can get information from around the world without leaving home.

notes: It is limited to a few fixed combinations such as 「生まれ・涙・昔・いつも・居（い）」 and cannot be used to build sentences freely: ✕「笑顔ながらに話した」 → ○「笑顔で話した」.
Here 「ながら」 means “just as it is,” not “while doing...,” and it has no concessive sense: 「昔ながらの店」 is “a shop that keeps its old ways,” not “old, but...”.
「涙ながらに」 goes only with speaking verbs such as 「語る・訴える・謝る」: ✕「涙ながらに走った」 → ○「泣きながら走った」.
Before a noun use 「の」; before a verb use 「に（して）」: ○「生まれながらの才能」「生まれながらにして持つ権利」.

daily.title: Walking an old street
daily.description: Admiring the scenery while strolling with a friend.
daily.example: This shopping street has a nice old-fashioned feel.

daily.title: Watching a documentary
daily.description: Talking about a story told in a TV documentary.
daily.example: An old woman was talking about the war in tears.

daily.title: Shopping online
daily.description: Telling family how convenient online shopping is.
daily.example: These days you can buy anything without leaving home.

work.title: Product promotion
work.description: Food packaging or ads describing traditional methods.
work.example: At our shop, we make our soba by hand in the traditional way.

work.title: News report
work.description: Reporting what someone said at a press conference.
work.example: The company president apologized in tears at the press conference.

etymology: 「ながら」 comes from classical Japanese and originally meant “just as it is, unchanged.” Today it usually means “while doing,” but 「ながらに」 keeps the old “unchanged” meaning in a few set phrases.

similar.title: 〜ながら
similar.explanation: Same origin: it is the same 「ながら」. 「〜ながら」 follows the verb's ます-stem and means two actions happening at the same time (「音楽を聞きながら勉強する」); 「〜ながらに」 keeps the old sense of “as it is” and is used only with fixed words such as 「生まれ・涙・昔」.

similar.title: 〜まま
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both mean keeping as is. 「〜まま」 can freely follow the た-form of a verb or 「noun + の」 (「靴のまま入る」); 「〜ながらに」 is limited to fixed combinations, is more literary, and often carries a nostalgic or admiring tone.

formation: It is 「ながら」 + the particle 「に」 (modifying a verb) or 「の」 (modifying a noun). The old meaning of 「ながら」 is “keeping as it is, just like...,” so 「生まれながら」 means “as one was when born,” 「昔ながら」 “as it was in the past,” and 「涙ながら」 “in a state of shedding tears.” Modern 「〜ながら」 has mostly become “while doing...,” and this “unchanged” old sense survives only in these set expressions, so the preceding word cannot be freely swapped. Add 「に」 to modify an action (「涙ながらに語る」) and 「の」 to modify a noun (「昔ながらの町並み」); the 「して」 in 「いながらにして」 further stresses “right in that state.”

meaning: Without something, the second part is hard to achieve. It stresses that the first part is essential.
connection: Noun + なくして (は) + negative expression

senses.label: Impossible without
senses.meaning: The first part is a necessary condition for the second. The second part is usually negative, 「ありえない」, 「難しい」, or a rhetorical question. Formal and written.
senses.connection: Noun (努力・協力・理解・愛, etc.) + なくして (は) + 〜ない／ありえない
examples: There is no success without effort.
Without everyone's cooperation, this project could never have happened.
You can't build a good relationship without trust.

senses.label: Can't talk about it without
senses.meaning: 「〜なくしては語れない」 means you can't discuss something without mentioning the first part. It stresses how important it is.
senses.connection: Noun + なくしては語れない／考えられない
examples: You can't tell the history of this town without the railway.
This championship would be unthinkable without his outstanding play.

notes: The second clause must be negative or mean “impossible”; with an affirmative it does not work: ✕「努力なくして成功した」 → ○「努力なくして成功はありえない」.
It is easily confused with the te-form of the verb 「なくす」 (“to lose”): 「財布をなくして困った」 is “I lost my wallet and was in trouble.” This pattern has no 「を」 before it and follows a noun directly: 「努力なくして」.
A verb cannot come directly before it: ✕「努力するなくして」 → ○「努力することなくして」 or 「努力なくして」.
It is very formal and literary, suited to speeches and thanks (「皆様のご支援なくしては、今日の成功はありませんでした」). In daily conversation people say 「〜がなければ」; 「なくして」 would sound exaggerated and stiff.

daily.title: A favorite quote
daily.description: Sharing a saying from a book with a friend.
daily.example: I like the saying “No joy without hardship.”

daily.title: Family support
daily.description: Thanking your parents at graduation.
daily.example: Without my parents' support, I wouldn't be who I am today.

work.title: A speech
work.description: Thanking the team at a project celebration.
work.example: Without all of your hard work, this success would not have been possible.

work.title: Company philosophy
work.description: A company profile stressing customer trust.
work.example: Without our customers' trust, our company cannot grow.

work.title: Academic paper
work.description: Arguing for the importance of a factor in a paper.
work.example: Without the understanding of local residents, it will be difficult to move the plan forward.

etymology: 「なくして」 is 「なく」, the continuative form of the classical adjective 「なし」, plus the particle 「して」. It's like modern 「なくて」: “in a state of not having ...”.

similar.title: 〜なしに（は）／〜なしでは
similar.explanation: Close in meaning and same origin (both from archaic 「なし」). 「〜なしには／なしでは」 can also mean “cannot do without...,” in both writing and speech; 「〜なしに」 can also simply mean “doing it without...” (「断りなしに使う」), while 「〜なくして」 is used only for “impossible without...” and is more formal.

similar.title: 〜あっての
similar.explanation: Close in meaning but from the opposite direction: 「AあってのB」 says positively “B exists only thanks to A” (「お客様あっての商売」); 「AなくしてBない」 says negatively “without A there is no B” (「お客様なくして商売は成り立たない」).

similar.title: 〜抜きで・〜抜きにして
similar.explanation: 「〜抜きでは／抜きにしては〜ない」 can also mean “can't do without...” (「彼抜きでは語れない」), but 「抜き」 originally means “deliberately leaving out,” so it is more colloquial; 「なくして」 stresses that the first item itself is an indispensable condition and is more formal.

similar.title: 〜ないことには
similar.explanation: Close in meaning. 「〜ないことには」 follows the verb's ない-form and means “can't... unless you first...” (「使ってみないことには分からない」); 「〜なくして」 follows a noun, stresses that something's existence is indispensable, and is more literary.

formation: It is the 連用形 「なく」 of the archaic adjective 「なし」 (“not exist”) + the conjunctive particle 「して」, which corresponds to modern 「て」, so 「Aなくして」 ≈ 「Aがなくて」, “in a state without A.” Followed by a negative or “impossible,” it becomes “in a state without A, B cannot hold,” that is, “without A there is no B,” stressing that A is an indispensable prerequisite. Adding 「は」 (「なくしては」) singles out “the case without A” for emphasis and is stronger. Since 「して」 is an archaic connective form, the whole is literary and formal.

meaning: Doing something without something; or, that something can't be done without it.
connection: Noun + なしに (は)／なしでは／なしで

senses.label: Did it without
senses.meaning: Someone did something without going through a step that should have come first. Often sounds annoyed or critical.
senses.connection: Noun (断り・連絡・予告・許可・休み, etc.) + なしに
examples: He used my computer without asking.
The meeting was canceled without any advance notice.
I worked ten hours straight without a break.

senses.label: Can't without
senses.meaning: 「〜なしには」 and 「〜なしでは」 are followed by a negative, showing the first part is essential.
senses.connection: Noun + なしには／なしでは + 〜ない／できない
examples: Without his help, this project would not have succeeded.
I can't study Japanese without this dictionary.
More and more people can't live without their smartphones.

notes: 「〜なしに」 (“doing it without...”) and 「〜なしには／なしでは〜ない」 (“can't do it without...”) mean different things: 「許可なしに入った」 is “entered without permission,” and 「許可なしには入れない」 is “can't enter without permission.”
It follows a noun directly; with a verb you need 「ことなしに」: ✕「連絡するなしに」 → ○「連絡なしに」「連絡することなしに」.
When 「断りなしに」 or 「連絡なしに」 describes someone else's behavior, it clearly sounds like blame. Said about a superior or client it comes across as accusing them, so soften it in the workplace.
In everyday situations like ordering or shopping, use 「〜なしで」: ○「砂糖なしでお願いします」. 「砂糖なしに」 sounds unnatural.

daily.title: Ordering a drink
daily.description: Making a request when ordering at a café.
daily.example: A coffee without sugar, please.

daily.title: Complaining about a roommate
daily.description: Telling a friend your roommate uses your things freely.
daily.example: My roommate wears my clothes without asking.

daily.title: Daily habits
daily.description: Talking about something you can't do without.
daily.example: I can't wake up in the morning without coffee.

work.title: Company rules
work.description: Company rules stating that permission is required.
work.example: Taking documents outside the company without permission is prohibited.

work.title: Project wrap-up
work.description: Thanking a partner company at a review meeting.
work.example: Without your company's support, we could not have achieved these results.

etymology: 「なし」 is the end form of the classical adjective meaning “none.” It works like a noun here and takes 「に」 or 「で」: “in a state of having no ...”.

similar.title: 〜なくして（は）
similar.explanation: Same origin (both from archaic 「なし」). 「〜なくして（は）」 only means “impossible without...” and is more formal; 「〜なしに」 can also simply describe “doing it without...” and works in both speech and writing.

similar.title: 〜ことなしに
similar.explanation: Same origin: it is the form 「なしに」 takes after a verb. 「連絡なしに」 follows a noun and 「連絡することなしに」 follows 「verb dictionary form + こと」. The meaning is the same, but the latter is more literary.

similar.title: 〜抜きで・〜抜きにして
similar.explanation: Close in meaning. 「〜抜きで」 means deliberately leaving out something that would normally be there (「朝ご飯抜きで出かけた」「冗談抜きで」); 「〜なしに」 only states the absence and does not stress that it was left out on purpose.

formation: It is the archaic adjective 「なし」 (“not exist”) + the particle 「に／で」. Here 「なし」 acts as a noun-like element meaning “a state without ...,” and 「に」「で」 indicate the state in which the action takes place, so 「Aなしに〜する」 means “do something in a state without A,” often skipping a step that should have been taken, which gives it a tone of blame. Adding the topic particle 「は」 gives 「なしには／なしでは」, singling out “the case without A,” and with a negative it means “can't do without A.”

meaning: Something unique that only a certain person, place, or thing has. Carries high praise.
connection: Noun + ならではの + noun／ならではだ

senses.label: Unique to
senses.meaning: Modifies a noun: “that only ... has.” Often used to praise local specialties or personal style.
senses.connection: Noun (place name, person, 手作り, etc.) + ならではの + noun
examples: This is scenery you can only find in Kyoto.
It has a warmth that only handmade things have.
I got information that only a local would know.

senses.label: Only ... could
senses.meaning: As a predicate: “only ... could do this.” Often in the pattern 「〜のは〜ならではだ」.
senses.connection: 〜のは + noun + ならではだ
examples: Only young people could come up with such a bold idea.
Such attentive service is something only a long-established inn can offer.

senses.label: No one but ... can
senses.meaning: 「〜ならでは〜ない」 means “no one but ... can do it.” Old-fashioned and written.
senses.connection: Noun + ならでは + verb nai-form
examples: Only my mother can make it taste like this.

notes: Use it only for positive evaluation and praise, never for negative things: ✕「都会ならではの騒音」 → ○「都会特有の騒音」. Saying 「新人ならではのミスだ」 is not only a misuse but will also feel like mockery to the person.
Do not confuse it with the conditional 「なら」: 「京都ならではの風景」 is “scenery that only Kyoto has,” not “if it's Kyoto.”
When praising someone, 「田中さんならではのアイデアですね」 is tactful. Forms like 「ならでは〜ない」 (「〜ならでは出せない」) are old-fashioned; in daily use, just 「ならではの」 or 「ならではだ」 is enough.

daily.title: Traveling
daily.description: Tasting a local specialty and raving about it with a friend.
daily.example: We enjoyed fresh seafood you can only get in Hokkaido.

daily.title: Complimenting a friend
daily.description: Praising a friend's work for its personal style.
daily.example: This use of color is so you.

daily.title: Seasonal activities
daily.description: Talking about Japan's seasonal traditions.
daily.example: Cherry blossom viewing is a pleasure only spring can bring.

work.title: Ad copy
work.description: A travel brochure introducing local specialties.
work.example: We offer local dishes you can only taste here.

work.title: Product description
work.description: Presenting a company's technical strengths.
work.example: With skills only a long-established maker has, we carefully finish each piece by hand.

etymology: 「なら」 is a form of the classical copula 「なり」, 「で」 is a classical negative connector (“without ...”), and 「は」 adds emphasis. Literally “if it isn't ..., (it won't do),” which came to mean “only ... has it.”

similar.title: 〜らしい(typical, fitting)
similar.explanation: Close in meaning. 「〜らしい」 means “having the typical features one expects of ...” (「春らしい天気」) and only says whether something fits; 「〜ならでは」 stresses uniqueness, “only it has this,” and is a higher praise.

similar.title: 〜をおいて
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both express “the only one.” 「〜をおいて（ほかに）〜ない」 says “there is no one else besides A,” mostly in evaluating candidates (「彼をおいてほかにいない」); 「〜ならでは（の）」 says that a certain character belongs only to A.

similar.title: 〜だけあって
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both carry praise. 「〜だけあって」 means “as you'd expect of...,” with a result that fits the status (「プロだけあってうまい」); 「〜ならでは」 stresses a uniqueness found nowhere else.

formation: It is 「なら」, the 未然形 of the archaic copula 「なり」, + 「で」, an archaic negative connective particle (“not... and”) + the topic particle 「は」. 「Aならでは」 literally means “if it is not A,” and was originally followed by a negative: 「Aならでは〜ない」 = “can't be done unless it's A,” i.e. “only A can.” Modern usage usually drops the negative half and uses 「Aならではの＋noun」 directly, which fixes the meaning as “something only A has.” Since the original structure says “nothing but A will do,” the first item is naturally raised to a unique position, giving it a high evaluation and limiting it to praise.

meaning: As soon as one action happens, a second, unexpected action follows right away.

senses.label: As soon as
senses.meaning: Two actions happen almost at once. The second is usually sudden or surprising. Both parts have the same subject; usually used to describe a third person.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + なり (common: 「帰るなり」, 「見るなり」, 「聞くなり」, 「言うなり」)
examples: As soon as he got home, he collapsed onto the bed.
The moment my daughter saw my face, she burst into tears.
The department head sat down and immediately started reading the documents.

notes: The second clause cannot be the speaker's volition, command, or request: ✕「家に帰るなり電話してください」 → ○「家に帰ったらすぐ電話してください」 or 「帰り次第電話してください」.
It is generally not used for the speaker's own actions: ✕「私は家に帰るなり寝た」 → ○「家に帰るとすぐ寝た」.
「〜たなり」, with the た-form, has almost the opposite meaning: 「部屋に入るなり泣き出した」 is “burst into tears the moment (she) entered the room”; 「部屋に入ったなり出てこない」 is “went into the room and hasn't come out since.”
Distinguish it from 「〜なり〜なり」 (“either... or...”): when a second 「なり」 follows (「電話するなりメールするなり」), it means choosing one of the two, not “as soon as.”

daily.title: Talking about family
daily.description: Telling a friend what your little brother does when he gets home.
daily.example: The minute my brother got home, he opened the fridge.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: A novel describing a character's strong reaction.
daily.example: As soon as she read the letter, she ran out of the room.

work.title: Talking about the boss
work.description: Coworkers discussing their manager's impatience.
work.example: The section chief started preparing for the meeting the moment he arrived at the office.

work.title: News report
work.description: Reporting someone's reaction to news.
work.example: As soon as the athlete heard the result, he sank to the ground right there.

etymology: Generally thought to come from the classical copula 「なり」. After a verb, it meant “just like that, as it is,” which developed into “right after ..., immediately ...”.

similar.title: 〜や否や／〜や
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both mean “as soon as...”, and neither allows volition or commands in the second clause. 「〜や否や」 is more literary and common in news and fiction, and the second item can be a natural phenomenon (「ベルが鳴るや否や」); 「〜なり」 mostly describes an unexpected act that a person does right afterward.

similar.title: 〜が早いか
similar.explanation: Close in meaning. 「〜が早いか」 stresses that the second event appears almost simultaneously with the first, highlighting speed; 「〜なり」 focuses on the unexpected act immediately following the first action.

similar.title: 〜たとたん（に）
similar.explanation: Close in meaning. 「〜たとたん」 follows the た-form, is common in speech, and the second item is mostly an unexpected change; it can also be about oneself (「立ち上がったとたん、めまいがした」). 「〜なり」 follows the dictionary form, is more literary, and mostly describes another person's spontaneous act.

similar.title: 〜次第(as soon as)
similar.explanation: Close in meaning but used the opposite way: 「〜次第」 means “as soon as..., (I will) do it right away,” and its second item is the speaker's own volition or request (「着き次第連絡します」); 「〜なり」 cannot take volition or requests in the second clause.

formation: It is the dictionary form of a verb + 「なり」. 「なり」 is generally thought to come from the archaic copula 「なり」, meaning “just so, exactly like that.” 「Aするなり」 means “right as A becomes a fact, (it goes) straight on to...,” with no gap or turn between the two actions, hence “as soon as... then...” Because the dictionary form is used, the stress is on the very moment A has just happened; the second item is often an unexpected act done by the person on the spot, a description of the scene before one's eyes, so it is mostly used in the third person and does not take the speaker's volition or commands.

meaning: Pick any one of the examples: “... or ..., just do something.”
connection: Noun／verb dictionary form + なり + noun／verb dictionary form + なり

senses.label: Either ... or ...
senses.meaning: Gives two examples to choose from: “either one is fine, but do something.” The second part is usually advice, a command, a request, or an intention.
senses.connection: Noun + なり + noun + なり (+ で／を); verb dictionary form + なり、verb dictionary form + なり + して
examples: If anything is unclear, please contact us by phone or email.
Look it up in a dictionary or ask your teacher. Find out for yourself.
Do whatever you want with me.

senses.label: ... or something
senses.meaning: 「〜なり何なり」 gives just one example and sums up the rest with 「何なり」: “... or whatever.”
senses.connection: Noun + なり何なり (なんなり)
examples: Get some drinks ready, like coffee or something.
At least on your day off, why not go see a movie or something?

notes: The second clause is usually advice, a command, a request, or volition, and it is not used to narrate past facts: ✕「昨日は本なり雑誌なり読んだ」 → ○「昨日は本や雑誌を読んだ」.
It has a “either is fine, do as you like” tone. Telling a superior or client 「電話なりメールなりで連絡してください」 sounds casual, like giving orders; in formal settings say 「お電話またはメールにてご連絡ください」.
「煮るなり焼くなり好きにしろ」 is a set phrase meaning “do whatever you want with me,” said in a defiant, reckless mood. Do not use it as an ordinary “choose either.”
Distinguish it from 「〜なり（一……就）」: 「帰るなり寝た」 has only one 「なり」 and means “fell asleep as soon as (he) got home.” This pattern needs two items, or 「〜なり何なり」.

daily.title: Advising a friend
daily.description: Encouraging a friend who's feeling down to do something.
daily.example: Don't just sit there feeling down. Why not take a walk or get some sleep?

daily.title: Parent to child
daily.description: A parent reminding a child to get in touch if they'll be late.
daily.example: If you're going to be late, give me a call or send a message.

daily.title: Planning a party
daily.description: Deciding what drinks to get.
daily.example: For drinks, just buy some juice or tea, whatever.

work.title: Boss's instructions
work.description: A manager telling staff to check an issue quickly.
work.example: Ask the person in charge or look through the documents, and confirm it soon.

work.title: How to submit
work.description: Explaining how documents can be submitted.
work.example: Please submit the documents by mail or in person.

etymology: From the classical copula 「なり」, used to list examples: “be it ... or be it ...”.

similar.title: 〜とか〜とか
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both list examples in parallel. 「〜とか〜とか」 is just a casual listing and can also be used for past facts (「本とか雑誌とか読んだ」); 「〜なり〜なり」 stresses “choose one of them and do it,” and the second clause is mostly advice or a command.

similar.title: 〜やら〜やら
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both list items. 「〜やら〜やら」 mostly lists things that have already happened, messy or tiring (「掃除やら洗濯やらで忙しい」); 「〜なり〜なり」 is for choices not yet made.

similar.title: 〜にしろ〜にしろ・〜にしても〜にしても
similar.explanation: Often compared. 「〜にしろ〜にしろ」 means “in either case the conclusion is the same” (「行くにしろ行かないにしろ、連絡してください」); 「〜なり〜なり」 means “pick one of them and do it.”

formation: It is two parallel units, 「A＋なり」 and 「B＋なり」. 「なり」 comes from the archaic copula and corresponds to “be it ...,” so 「AなりBなり」 literally means “be it A or be it B.” Approving each option in turn amounts to “either is fine,” and the point is not the listing itself but “anyway, do something,” so the second clause is usually advice, a command, or volition. When only one item is given, use 「Aなり何なり」, with 「何」 covering the rest: “A or whatever.”

meaning: In a way that matches someone's or something's ability, position, or situation: limited, but to a fitting degree.
connection: Noun／verb plain form／i-adjective + なりに (なりの + noun)

senses.label: In one's own way
senses.meaning: Doing one's best within one's ability or position. It admits limits but still gives some credit. Sounds modest when used about yourself.
senses.connection: Noun (私・子ども・彼, etc.) + なりに + verb／なりの + noun (考え・理由, etc.)
examples: I believe I did my very best, in my own way.
Kids have their own worries too.
He probably has his own reasons.

senses.label: Fitting the situation
senses.meaning: Matching the situation or conditions in the first part. The first part is often a drawback: “although ..., it has its own corresponding ...”. 「それなりに」 means “reasonably, decently.”
senses.connection: I-adjective／verb plain form + なりに／なりの; それなりに
examples: This room is small, but it's easy to use for its size.
The quality was about what you'd expect for the low price.
We didn't have much time to prepare, but it went reasonably well.

notes: Do not use it to evaluate a superior or elder, or it sounds like condescendingly “grading” them: ✕「社長なりに頑張っている」 → ○「社長も大変努力していらっしゃる」. Used about yourself (「私なりに」), it is appropriately modest.
It implies limited ability or conditions, so evaluating someone else with it easily sounds dismissive: telling a coworker 「田中さんなりに頑張ったね」 may be taken as “that's about all you could do.”
「それなりに」 leans toward “passably good”: saying 「それなりにいいですね」 about someone's work sounds perfunctory; say 「とてもいいですね」 directly.

daily.title: Comforting a friend
daily.description: Comforting a friend who did badly on an exam.
daily.example: I think you worked really hard, in your own way.

daily.title: A secondhand item
daily.description: Telling family about a cheap item you bought.
daily.example: It's secondhand, but it's pretty clean.

daily.title: Talking about kids
daily.description: Parents talking about their child's thinking.
daily.example: Our kid seems to be thinking about the future in their own way.

work.title: Submitting a report
work.description: Modestly explaining your analysis to a manager.
work.example: I tried analyzing the market trends in my own way.

work.title: Reviewing a budget
work.description: Explaining results achieved on a limited budget.
work.example: The budget was small, but we got creative and delivered results.

etymology: 「なり」 was originally the noun 「形（なり）」, “shape, appearance.” It came to mean “in keeping with its appearance,” and from there “in a way that suits ...”.

similar.title: 〜らしい(typical, fitting)
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both relate to “A's characteristics.” 「〜らしい」 means “having the typical look that A should have” (「学生らしい服装」); 「〜なりに」 means “within A's limited ability and conditions (doing one's best, correspondingly),” implying a limitation.

similar.title: 〜に応じて
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both mean “in accordance with...” 「〜に応じて」 is more objective, adjusting as conditions change (「能力に応じて給料を払う」); 「〜なりに」 carries a subjective evaluation: “limited, but with a corresponding degree.”

similar.title: 〜た分だけ
similar.explanation: Close in meaning. 「〜た分だけ」 stresses a proportional match in quantity (「努力した分だけ結果が出る」); 「〜なりの」 stresses a degree or quality that suits the conditions (「安いなりの品質」), often with the nuance “about what you'd expect.”

formation: It is the noun 「なり」 (“shape, form”) + the particle 「に／の」. 「なり」 originally means “appearance, figure,” and by extension “a degree that suits that figure.” 「Aなりに」 means “in keeping with A's form and scale,” i.e. within the range of A's ability and position; 「Aなりの＋noun」 means “... that suits A.” Because “according to A's scale” assumes that A has limits, it often carries the nuance “limited, but with its own corresponding ...”: modest when used about oneself, and slightly reserved when about others.

meaning: Being in a special period, position, or situation.

senses.label: In the midst of
senses.meaning: In a special situation, era, or position. The second part explains the fitting state or action in that situation. 「にあっては」 emphasizes the special setting.
senses.connection: Noun (時代・状況・立場・非常時, etc.) + にあって (は)
examples: In a recession like this, increasing sales is not easy.
In modern society, how we handle information is important.
In an emergency, calm judgment is required.

senses.label: Even in
senses.meaning: 「にあっても」 is contrastive: “even in a tough situation like ..., still ...”. Often used to praise someone's strength.
senses.connection: Noun (逆境・困難な状況, etc.) + にあっても
examples: Even in adversity, he never lost hope.
She's the kind of person who never forgets to smile, no matter how hard things get.

notes: Use it only for special eras, situations, or positions, not for ordinary places: ✕「この部屋にあって勉強した」 → ○「この部屋で勉強した」.
Distinguish it from the similar-looking 「〜にあたって」 (“on the occasion of...”): ✕「出発にあって、挨拶をした」 → ○「出発にあたって、挨拶をした」.
「〜にあっては」 means “precisely because one is in...,” while 「〜にあっても」 is concessive, “even in...”, so the second clause goes in a different direction: 「逆境にあっても諦めない」 means “don't give up even in adversity.”
It is very literary. Saying 「この不況下にあって」 in everyday conversation sounds like a speech; in speech use 「〜の中で」 or 「〜では」.

daily.description: An expression found in a biography of a famous person.
daily.example: Even in poverty, he never stopped learning.

etymology: Made of the location particle 「に」 and the te-form of 「ある」 (to exist). Literally “existing in ...”, which came to mean “being in the situation of ...”.

similar.title: 〜において
similar.explanation: Close in meaning. 「〜において」 only objectively marks where or in what field something happens (「会議において決定した」); 「〜にあって」 stresses being in a particular situation or position, which affects the second clause.

similar.title: 〜中を・〜中では（なか）
similar.explanation: Close in meaning. 「〜中を」 means doing something in a concrete, mostly unfavorable situation (「雨の中を出かけた」「お忙しい中を」); 「〜にあって」 is more literary and mostly refers to abstract circumstances such as an era or a position.

similar.title: 〜のもとで・〜のもとに
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both mean “under...”. 「〜のもとで」 stresses being under someone's guidance or influence, or under certain conditions (「先生のもとで学ぶ」); 「〜にあって」 stresses the circumstance one is in.

formation: It is the particle 「に」 (place, situation) + the te-form 「あって」 of the verb 「ある」 (“exist”), literally “being within A.” With an abstract noun such as an era, situation, or position as A, it becomes “in the situation of A,” and the second clause describes the state or conduct in that circumstance. Adding 「は」 (「にあっては」) singles out the circumstance, “precisely because one is in this circumstance”; adding 「も」 (「にあっても」) makes it concessive, “even though in it.” Since it uses 「ある」, which expresses existence, rather than 「で」, which marks where an action happens, it stresses the state of “being placed in a certain circumstance.”

meaning: From a group of similar things, picks out the most extreme example: “as for ..., it's even worse.”

senses.label: As for ..., even worse
senses.meaning: First describe the overall situation, then use this to give the most extreme example. Usually negative, with surprise or exasperation.
senses.connection: Noun + に至っては + extreme situation (「まったく〜ない」, 「〜さえ〜」, etc.)
examples: I'm bad at math. As for physics, I don't understand it at all.
My whole family was against it. My father even stopped talking to me.
Sales fell this year. At our regional stores, they were less than half of last year's.

notes: There must first be a general statement; this phrase is just the single most extreme example and cannot start a sentence alone: ○「数学も苦手だが、物理に至っては、まったくわからない」.

The person or thing singled out becomes “the worst one,” with a clearly negative evaluation. Saying 「部長に至っては…」 about a boss or coworker at work amounts to criticizing them behind their back, which is very rude.

Distinguish it from the related 「〜に至って」 and 「〜に至っても」: 「事故に至って初めて」 is “only when it got as far as an accident,” 「事故に至っても」 is “even when it got as far as an accident,” and 「彼に至っては」 is “as for him, it's even worse.”

etymology: 「至る」 means “to reach.” 「に至っては」 literally means “when it comes to reaching this point,” which came to mean “as for the most extreme case ...”.

similar.title: 〜ときたら
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both bring up a person or thing in order to evaluate it negatively. 「〜ときたら」 raises the topic directly to vent complaints (「うちの夫ときたら」) and is strongly colloquial; 「〜に至っては」 first states the whole picture and then picks out the most extreme case, and is more literary.

similar.title: 〜まで(even)
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both show a degree beyond expectation. 「〜まで」 follows a noun directly to mean “even...” (「子どもまで笑った」); 「〜に至っては」 sets the most extreme example apart as a topic, and the second clause explains how serious it is.

similar.title: 〜に至る／〜に至って
similar.explanation: Same origin. 「〜に至る」 means that things finally develop to a certain extent (「戦争に至った」); 「〜に至っては」 is used to pick the most extreme example within a group.

similar.title: 〜に至っても
similar.explanation: Same origin. 「〜に至っても」 means “even when things have reached...(still no change),” and is mostly critical; 「〜に至っては」 means “as for... it's even worse” and is used for giving an example.

formation: It is the particle 「に」 + the te-form of the verb 「至る」 (“to reach”) + the topic particle 「は」. 「Aに至って」 means “reaching the point of A,” and with 「は」 it is raised as a topic, literally “when it comes to the point of A.” Counting through a series of similar things “all the way to A,” A naturally becomes the last and most extreme item, so it is used to pick out the most extreme example. The second clause often has 「まったく〜ない」 or 「〜さえ〜」, bringing out surprise or resignation that “it has even come to this.”

meaning: A situation finally develops to a serious point. 「〜に至って」 means “only when it reached that point did ...”.
connection: Noun／verb dictionary form + に至る／に至った／に至って

senses.label: End up reaching
senses.meaning: After a process, something reaches a certain result or stage. Usually something serious or major. Often with 「ついに」 or 「ようやく」.
senses.connection: Noun／verb dictionary form + に至る／に至った; 〜に至った経緯
examples: The conflict between the two countries finally led to war.
After a long discussion, they finally reached an agreement.
I'd like you to explain how it came to the point where he quit the company.

senses.label: Only when it reached
senses.meaning: 「〜に至って（初めて／ようやく）」 means only after things got serious did someone act or realize something. Implies criticism: “too late.”
senses.connection: Noun／verb dictionary form + に至って (初めて／ようやく)
examples: Only after an accident happened were the safety measures finally reviewed.
Only on the verge of death did he finally tell the truth.

senses.label: Leading to
senses.meaning: Physically reaching a place. Mostly used to describe roads or routes; written style.
senses.connection: Place noun + に至る + noun (道・ルート, etc.)
examples: The path to the summit is steep.

notes: The second item is mostly a major, serious development or formal result; used for small daily matters it sounds exaggerated: ✕「昼ご飯を食べるに至った」 → ○「昼ご飯を食べることになった」.
「〜に至って（初めて／ようやく）」 carries criticism of being too late. Saying it about the other person or their company accuses them of a slow response, so use it carefully with clients and superiors.
The negative 「〜に至らない」 often expresses relief: 「大事には至らなかった」 means “it didn't turn into a serious matter,” not “failed to reach a big matter.”
Distinguish it from the related 「〜に至るまで」: 「子どもから大人に至るまで」 means “from children to adults, all,” expressing a range, not “finally developing into...”.

etymology: 「至る」 originally means “to arrive.” From physically reaching a place, it came to mean a situation developing over time to a certain point.

similar.title: 〜に及んで
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both mean “having reached the point of... (only then)”. 「〜に及んで」 stresses that the situation has already worsened and is hard to reverse (「この期に及んで」); 「〜に至って」 focuses on “only at this stage did it finally...”.

similar.title: 〜末(に)
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both give the result after a process. 「〜末に」 stresses a long period of thought, effort, or twists (「悩んだ末に決めた」); 「〜に至る」 stresses the final stage reached, mostly a major development.

similar.title: 〜あげく
similar.explanation: Close in meaning. 「〜あげく」 means that after much agonizing or fuss the result is mostly bad, with the speaker's regret or dissatisfaction; 「〜に至る」 merely describes the situation finally reached, good or bad (「合意に至った」).

similar.title: 〜に至るまで
similar.explanation: Same origin. 「〜に至るまで」 means “from... to... all,” stressing a wide range (「細部に至るまで」); 「〜に至る」 means that things finally develop to a certain extent.

formation: It is the particle 「に」, marking the point reached, + the verb 「至る」 (“to reach”). 「至る」 originally means spatially “arrive at a place” (「山頂に至る道」); replacing the destination with a situation gives “after a process, finally reaching a certain stage or result,” so it often pairs with 「ついに」「ようやく」. In the te-form 「に至って」, 「て」 introduces “having reached this point” as the premise of the second clause, and adding 「初めて／ようやく」 gives “only after reaching this point,” implying criticism that nothing had been done until then. Since 「至る」 is itself a formal literary word, the whole is mostly used in formal styles such as news and reports.
